intent: Express each piece of knowledge in a system exactly once, so a rule or structure that changes has one authoritative home and every duplicate site fails loudly when it drifts.
problem: The same business rule, validation, protocol definition, constant table or SQL fragment is restated in several places, so a change to the rule must be applied correctly in all of them; forgetting one site produces divergent behaviour that no compiler flags, because the duplication is textual rather than typed.
context: Applies wherever knowledge is restated: two functions that must stay in step, a constant repeated across modules, an error message repeated in a handler and a log, a schema repeated in code and in documentation, a regex pasted into three services. The unit of duplication is knowledge, not text — two blocks that look alike but encode different rules are not duplicates, and two identical-looking blocks that encode one rule are.
benefits: A change to a rule is made once; every call site picks it up by construction.
Divergence between duplicates becomes impossible rather than merely unlikely.
Duplicated logic is also duplicated test coverage; one tested implementation is one test suite.
Duplicated identifiers are a reliable source of copy-paste defects that reviewers routinely miss.
Extraction often reveals that the two sites were never actually the same, which is itself valuable information.
tradeoffs: The cost of a violation is the cost of maintenance of the extracted abstraction plus the risk that it is the wrong abstraction, paid on every third duplicate.
Premature DRY is the common failure: abstracting at the second occurrence bakes in an assumption that two examples cannot falsify.
Some duplication is deliberate — cryptographic code is safer when cross-checked against a second independent implementation.
Over-abstraction creates indirection and a parameterised helper that is harder to read than two concrete blocks.
Knowledge vs. text: shared tables or schemas may be duplicated for independent deployability, at the cost of a manual synchronisation process.
quality_attributes_note: maintainability 9 is the whole point; simplicity 5 because aggressive DRY adds indirection. type_safety is not improved by DRY itself — it removes divergence risk, not type errors.

participants.responsibility: The rule or structure that must be stated once.
participants.notes: Text may legitimately appear more than once if the knowledge behind it is distinct.

participants.responsibility: The one place the knowledge is defined.
participants.notes: Typically a named constant, function, table or schema module.

participants.responsibility: A consumer that must reference rather than restate.
participants.notes: If a consumer cannot reference the home, the home is in the wrong module.

use_cases: Extracting the repeated date-formatting call from four report builders.
Hoisting a magic retry count used by three HTTP clients into a shared constant.
Generating enum-like constants from one table rather than restating each case.
Defining a validation rule once and reusing it in both the API layer and the batch import.
Deriving documentation and schema from a single definition instead of keeping both in sync by hand.
avoid_when: You have only two occurrences — see the rule of three; wait for the third.
The two blocks are superficially identical but encode different rules that happen to coincide today.
The "duplicate" is independently-verifiable security-critical code, where two implementations are a feature (diversification).
Independent deployability requires a duplicated schema or table; a runtime dependency is worse than a synchronisation process.
The shared abstraction would need a dozen parameters to cover both call sites — that is a sign they are not the same knowledge.
pitfalls: Abstracting at the second duplicate (premature DRY) locks in a wrong abstraction that later needs unwinding.
DRYing data instead of logic — merging two tables that record different facts into one with nullable columns.
A helper whose name cannot be written without "and" or "or" is two knowledge items pretending to be one.
Sharing a mutable global to satisfy DRY reintroduces exactly the coupling duplication was avoiding.
Copy-paste with a tiny edit is the hardest case for reviewers and the most common source of real defects.

related_patterns_notes.rule-of-three: Rule of Three is the timing rule that keeps DRY from firing prematurely; the two must be read together.
related_patterns_notes.collecting-parameter: The canonical DRY violation shape: several parameters travelling together through many functions signal one missing object.
related_patterns_notes.parameter-object: The DRY fix for a repeating parameter list, when the parameters genuinely belong together.

anti_patterns: A single "utils"/"common" module that grows into a dumping ground and becomes the most-coupled file in the codebase.
Boolean flag parameters (`isActive=true/false`) so one function can serve two different rules — duplication with worse ergonomics.
Copy-paste with a one-character edit that reviewers consistently miss.
Abstracting the second occurrence into a generic/template helper whose configuration surface exceeds the code it replaced.
A shared mutable constant imported everywhere, creating global coupling in the name of deduplication.
design_principles: Every piece of knowledge must have a single, unambiguous, authoritative representation in the system (Hunt & Thomas, 1999).
Once and only once (Beck) — the XP phrasing of the same rule.
Name the knowledge before extracting it; if the name resists, the extraction is wrong.
Design and implementation must agree (Hunt & Thomas) — a duplicated schema is duplicated knowledge.
best_practices: Apply DRY to knowledge, not to characters; identical text with different intent is fine.
Combine DRY with Rule of Three: wait for the third occurrence before extracting.
Extract into a name that reads as a concept at the call site.
Use generated code or schema-first definitions when the repetition is structural (many near-identical endpoints, table definitions).
Never share mutable state to satisfy DRY.
Run a duplication detector in CI and treat new clusters as review comments rather than automatic failures.
sources: Martin Fowler, Avoiding Repetition, IEEE Software 18(6), 2001 — https://www.martinfowler.com/ieeeSoftware/repetition.pdf
Martin Fowler, Refactoring: Improving the Design of Existing Code, 2nd ed., Addison-Wesley 2018 — https://martinfowler.com/books/refactoring.html
DRY (Don't Repeat Yourself) — Laws of Software Engineering — https://lawsofsoftwareengineering.com/laws/dry-principle
